name: Hemocytometer Cell Counter (cells/mL)
seoDesc: A hemocytometer turns a counted number of cells into a concentration using one physical fact: each large square holds 0.1 µL. Free hemocytometer cell counter
summary:
A hemocytometer turns a counted number of cells into a concentration using one physical fact: each large square holds 0.1 µL. It returns cell concentration, cell concentration, total cells in the suspension and concentration, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator averages your counts, applies the dilution factor — including the trypan blue step — and returns cells/mL, cells/µL and total cells. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hemocytometer Cell Counter (cells/mL)
sections.html:
Cells/mL = (cells counted ÷ squares counted) × dilution factor × 10⁴

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
cells_countedcells counted across all squarescells
squaresnumber of large squares counted—
dilutiontotal dilution before counting×
10⁴reciprocal of the 0.1 µL volume of one large squaremL⁻¹

Where the relationship comes from. Improved Neubauer chamber geometry; the counting convention is the standard haematology one.

sections.title: How do I use the Hemocytometer Cell Counter (cells/mL)?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: total cells counted of 320 cells, squares counted of 4, dilution factor of 2 ×, suspension volume of 10 mL.

Substituting them into the formula gives cell concentration of 1,600,000 cells/mL, cell concentration of 1,600 cells/µL, total cells in the suspension of 16,000,000 cells, concentration of 1.6 ×10⁶/mL.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
20 – 200 per squareCountablehigh enough for precision, low enough to resolve
below 20Too fewsampling error dominates; count more squares
above 200Too manyclumps and overlapping cells; dilute

  • The 10⁴ is geometry, not a correction: 1 mm × 1 mm × 0.1 mm = 0.1 mm³ = 10⁻⁴ mL.

  • Count the cells touching the top and left lines and skip the bottom and right ones, so border cells are counted exactly once.

  • Aim for 100–200 cells per large square. Below about 20, the Poisson counting error alone is 20% or worse.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Forgetting the trypan blue dilution — the single most common cause of a concentration that is exactly half the truth.
  • Counting clumps as single cells without disaggregating and re-counting.
  • Loading the chamber without letting it fill by capillary action, which leaves an uneven distribution.

faq.a: Because each large square holds 0.0001 mL, and dividing by such a small volume is the same as multiplying by 10 000.

faq.q: How many squares should I count?
faq.a: Four large corner squares is standard; count more if the cells are sparse.

faq.q: Does this work for the Fuchs–Rosenthal chamber?
faq.a: Not directly — that chamber is 0.2 mm deep, so the factor is 5 000 rather than 10 000.

faq.q: What does the Hemocytometer Cell Counter (cells/mL) actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns cell concentration, cell concentration, total cells in the suspension and concentration. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
